extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, students of fiction, and critics studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of novel-writing techniques focusing on narration, scene-setting, pacing, and the relation between descriptive preparation and dramatic effect, with examples from Balzac, Tolstoy, Dickens, Stevenson, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of first-person narration as dramatization
rubrics_metrics.description: The first person can be 'the first step towards the dramatization of a story' — placing events in the mouth of someone who was present and passing the drama through that person's thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enhances a plain narrative by working the drama into a picture and catching a man's reflection of it. Works differently with different subjects (example: Esmond vs The Master of Ballantrae). Use when you need the immediacy or the colouring of a participant's consciousness; beware that effect varies with subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary pictorial scene prepares the drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with a pictured scene that 'opens and spreads very gradually' to make a valid world and to store a reserve of force for the drama to come.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balzac's method: build the house/street/setting fully in advance so the later action is supported and the climax gains force. Use detailed, anticipatory description to give the drama ballast; this allows later narrative economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and fullness of descriptive detail
rubrics_metrics.description: A minute knowledge of the things and objects that surround characters — down to vases, pots and pans — is essential; description offered 'as an essential preliminary to the story'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions may be plain and inventory-like and still work if the author truly knows the scene. Provide exact, business-like detail early so the reader accepts the setting as authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internalized image versus mechanical listing
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions must come from possession of the scene in the writer's mind; otherwise adding fact to fact produces only a mechanical sum that makes no image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bare catalogues of detail unless the writer's imagination has already created the whole scene; when the image is internalized you can reproduce details 'inch by inch' without losing the overall effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting to incarnate character and social foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: A house, street, or building can incarnate a character's past and be an active influence in the story — 'the Maison Grandet ... incarnates all the past of its old owner'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make setting do narrative work: embody moral and social conditions, link past to present action, and supply meaning for characters' behaviour. Treat important settings as quasi-characters that participate in the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure sense of time through preparatory picture
rubrics_metrics.description: A thorough preliminary picture can already represent the passage and accumulation of time so that later years may be summarized without loss of effect (Balzac's 'Five years went by' works because of prior preparation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need to convey long durations with little incident, prepare by establishing routines, habits, and the sameness of life in the descriptive opening so that later chronological leaps feel credible and weighty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of climax — reserve and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax 'ought to complete, to add the touch that makes the book whole' and should be free to do its task without unnecessary distraction — prepare the climax in advance and let it perform only the necessary movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making the climax bear extraneous work (over-explaining or inventing sudden, artificial incidents). Let earlier preparation supply what the climax needs so it can be a precise, unforced stroke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invisible (unobtrusive) preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of preparation is 'no art if it betrays itself at the outset'; it should be unrecognizable until it achieves its end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not call attention to your preparatory devices. If preparation is 'tactless and obtrusive' it spoils the effect. Strive for subtle setup that the reader only perceives retrospectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to subject (method-subject fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The same narrative method has different effects according to the subject; choose pictorial exposition, scenic dramatization, or blended approaches depending on what the material demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Balzac's pictorial preparation suits slow, pictorial climaxes; Tolstoy's scenic, episodic method suits broad social-chronicle material. Assess your subject's needs before fixing narrative method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition with increasing intensity when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When a plot consists of reiterated failures or similar events (e.g., the progressive outbreaks in La Recherche de l'Absolu), the opening picture provides a resource so repetition is renewed and heightened rather than dulled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a rich initial scene whose progressive destruction or alteration can visually register escalation. Repetition can be powerful if each recurrence is shown against a changing, diminishing background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible point-of-view in large, episodic works
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed method — mostly scenic/dramatic presentation but with occasional direct revelation of characters' thought — enables handling many lives and episodes without losing intimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy's practice: keep the chronology and external scene but 'lay bare the mind' of characters when it aids force or lucidity. Use shifts sparingly to sustain both external action and inner access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of omitting pictorial introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: A refusal to provide any pictorial introduction can 'damage' a book by removing the timely precaution that some effects require (Tolstoy's Anna Karenina is cited as lacking pictorial introduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether your work needs an establishing picture; absence of such introduction may weaken certain kinds of effect (especially those relying on background, routine, or accumulated impression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy in creating characters within scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters can be created efficiently in a few words by catching passing thoughts and manner — 'each of them is a centre of vision' — so long as those touches reveal the nature of their experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise, telling details and momentary thoughts to render character quickly in scenes. This is a conscious technique of large-canvas writers handling many figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two strategies for rendering long, sparse spans: interiorization or pictorial preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: When little happens externally over long periods, a novelist can either dwell in the character's consciousness (interiorization) or prepare a pictorial scene that carries the sense of time; Balzac chooses the latter for Eugenie Grandet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose between deep interior focus to dramatize slow psychological change, or build an external picture whose constancy/monotony implies duration. Be aware each approach suits different subject-material and can change reader sympathy.
